surface cladding. `perimeter_dressing.py` generates `perimeter_dressing.json`;
the same file feeds the Blender preview and TST's runtime scenery swap through
`ce_upgrade_maps.json`. This makes a rock's intended transform inspectable and
reproducible. `inspect_native_decor.py` checks these render meshes against the
206 authored player envelopes, including the two roof ramps. Neither check validates Unreal collision shapes,
movement, vehicle physics or multiplayer balance.

The southern rock crown has explicit CLIFF face overrides: cladding is allowed
but grass is not, avoiding a continuous turf strip. Submerged pond faces use
NONE. Other cliff faces retain BOTH as their material default. Inspect the
`pcg.png` view or paint face overrides in the add-on to see this distinction.

Only LOD0 is displayed. Grass opacity uses the native packed texture's red
channel. Native mesh topology, texture images and placements are real game data;
Blender lighting, wind, layered materials and water are approximations. The
Desert/CliffFlat macro meshes use the authored coastal-granite preview material
instead of their Unreal layered shader. Source and placement hashes reject
stale preview manifests. Rebuild the local asset cache after game updates.

The recipe supports native `Lrg_A` tree assemblies, complete `Pine_Optimized`
and `Pine_Sapling_A` conifers, and an explicit `leaf_cluster_scale`. TST enlarges
the three basin trees' leaf clusters by 43% while preserving attachment
positions and pivots. Twenty-eight native conifers form eight small groups
behind the wall. Complete pine meshes use separate bark/needle material slots.
These settings affect the shared runtime recipe too. Background scenery
remains outside the playable enclosure.

Open `preview.blend` for a visual review and `tst.blend` for authoring. Keep the
entire `.dream-loop` cache and preview file out of the community source archive:
they contain extracted game content. Share the scripts, placement recipes,
authored geometry/textures, permissions and required asset paths instead.

TST additionally uses `foliage_cluster: {"grass": [12, 0.10, 0.60]}` and the matching
preview argument `--rule-cluster grass=12,0.10,0.60`. This creates deterministic
12 m density patches with smooth probabilistic edges between the two noise
thresholds. Other maps retain their default scatter rules. The Blender meadow
underlay and foliage shader colors are preview studies, separate from these
shared runtime placement settings.


## 5. Place objectives, equipment and lights

Red starts use team 0, blue team 1, and neutral starts -1. Place one flag per
team. Keep starts clear of walls and ceilings, with multiple escape directions.
Use unique teleporter channels; pair each sender with its receiver, and face
the arriving player away from obstructions or another sender boundary.
The TST balcony demonstrates a green walk-through shield: a render-only mesh
uses `example_tutorial_teleporter`, while separate scenario flags supply the
trigger and destination. Set `to_scenery: false` (or `scenery: false` for both
ends) to omit the stock floor pad where the doorway already supplies the visual.
For TST's 4.7 m wide doors, `shield_return: true` makes `prepare_runtime.py`
add two overlapping sender volumes beside the central one on the same channel.
This covers the whole doorway and raises the trigger to its 3.35 m height.
Keep the receiving position outside these volumes to avoid an immediate return.

Inspect light bitmaps before assigning UVs. `mp lights small strips` is a
1024x256 atlas of many fixtures, not a tileable strip. TST samples one capsule
at pixels (326,2)-(380,23), converts top-left image coordinates to Blender UVs,
and repeats separate quads along long lenses. Use the actual atlas in previews
so a flat emission color cannot conceal stretching or the wrong atlas region.

Place light fixtures as actual scenario objects. Colored trim identifies bases;
it does not replace readable interior lighting. Conversion with
`LIGHTMAP_ARGS=--placed-lights` includes fixtures in the light solve. Test final
interior illumination in game after the visual milestone.

TST's `objective_markers` specify the neutral ball and three moving hills.
`prepare_runtime.py` turns these into runtime labels. The rules, marker boundaries,
HUD and matching code-mod version must all agree before a mode is advertised.

## 6. Compile the CE cache

From the repository root in PowerShell 7:

```powershell
pwsh -File levels/test/tst/rebuild.ps1
# Or consume your hand-exported JMS and edited placements:
pwsh -File levels/test/tst/rebuild.ps1 -SkipGeometry
```

Override `-HekRoot`, `-BlenderExe`, `-PythonExe`, `-AddonRoot`, and `-MccTagsRoot`
for your machine. The add-on root ends in `io_scene_halo`.

The wrapper runs geometry export, Blender annotation, structure, scenario,
lightmaps and cache compilation. Read its logs under `.dream-loop/tst-rebuild/`.
It checks error text and fresh output timestamps because `tool.exe` can report
failure with exit code zero. Never continue with a stale map. It temporarily
moves `bitmaps.map` aside to embed lightmaps and restores it in `finally`.
The resulting cache is `<HEK>/maps/tst.map`.

### Experimental split facility build

The dense facility detail can exceed the classic HEK structure compiler's
limits. An **experimental** opt-in separates its render-only metal triangles
into a native mesh while retaining the complementary CE structure and collision.
This path has not yet been validated end to end in the game. Use a dedicated
HEK copy and a new output folder; never point it at your existing map outputs.
It requires Python with NumPy, Blender and the Halo add-on described above.

For example, in PowerShell 7, replace these paths for your machine. The work
folder must not already exist; the tag copy excludes only the old TST outputs.
The original kit is read, never modified by this preparation:

```powershell
$classic = 'C:/haloce/hek'
$work = 'C:/haloce/ce_conversions/tst-split-example'
if (Test-Path -LiteralPath $work) { throw "Choose a new work folder: $work" }
$hek = Join-Path $work 'hek'
$bundle = Join-Path $work 'bundle'
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $hek,(Join-Path $hek 'maps') | Out-Null
& robocopy (Join-Path $classic 'tags') (Join-Path $hek 'tags') /E /XJ /COPY:DAT /DCOPY:DAT /R:1 /W:1 /XD (Join-Path $classic 'tags/levels/test/tst')
if ($LASTEXITCODE -ge 8) { throw 'HEK tag copy failed; inspect the copy before continuing.' }
foreach ($name in @('tool.exe','ogg.dll','vorbis.dll','vorbisenc.dll','vorbisfile.dll')) {
    Copy-Item -LiteralPath (Join-Path $classic $name) -Destination (Join-Path $hek $name)
}
foreach ($name in @('bitmaps.map','sounds.map','loc.map')) {
    Copy-Item -LiteralPath (Join-Path $classic "maps/$name") -Destination (Join-Path $hek "maps/$name")
}
pwsh -File levels/test/tst/rebuild.ps1 -HekRoot $hek -SplitFacilityDetail -FacilityOutputDir $bundle
```

Override `-BlenderExe`, `-AddonRoot` and `-MccTagsRoot` when needed. The split
option requires a fresh full geometry export; it cannot be combined with
`-SkipGeometry`. It refuses an existing bundle or existing TST build outputs in
the dedicated HEK. The new bundle contains `authoring/tst.blend`, its owned
textures and `surfaces.json`, the full original JMS and placements, a separate
`partition/` with the reduced CE JMS and complementary native glTF/bin,
`tst.map`, and build evidence. The `.blend` references its bundled textures
through relative paths. The full authored JMS is never replaced by the reduced
one. A canonical `tst-facility-ce-build-receipt.json` is created only after
successful structure, scenario, lightmap and cache stages and receipt checks;
if the build fails, inspect the bundle and logs rather than reusing a prior map.

After this succeeds, set up the conversion environment in the next section,
then override its normal map and surface-library paths for this bundle:

```bash
export BUNDLE="C:/haloce/ce_conversions/tst-split-example/bundle"
export CE_SURFACE_LIBRARY="$BUNDLE/authoring/surfaces.json"
export CE_NATIVE_DETAIL="$BUNDLE/partition/tst-facility-detail.gltf"
export CE_NATIVE_SOURCE_JMS="$BUNDLE/authoring/data/levels/test/tst/models/tst.JMS"
export CE_NATIVE_BUILD_RECEIPT="$BUNDLE/tst-facility-ce-build-receipt.json"
bash tools/level/convert_ce_map.sh "$BUNDLE/tst.map" TST C:/haloce/ce_conversions/tst-split-example/converted/TST
```

The converter verifies the receipt and matching
material slots before cooking. Keep the map, partition, full JMS, surface
library and receipt from the same build together. Native placement, lighting,
collision, performance and multiplayer behavior still require in-game checks.

## 7. Convert and upgrade a visual milestone

Build the helper executables listed in [the rebuild reference](pipeline_test_map.md#tools-and-rebuild).
From Git Bash, set explicit paths to this revision's tools:

```bash
export TST_REPO="$(pwd -W)"
export HCE_GAME="C:/Program Files (x86)/Steam/steamapps/common/Halo Campaign Evolved"
export HCE_PAKS="$HCE_GAME/Meteorite/Content/Paks"
export MJOLNIR="$TST_REPO/target/release/mjolnir.exe"
export MJOLNIR_DEBUG="$MJOLNIR"
export MJOLNIR_EXAMPLES="$TST_REPO/target/release/examples"
export EXAMPLES="$TST_REPO/target/debug/examples"
export HALO2UE_EXPORT="C:/your-tools/halo2ue-export.exe"
export PYTHONUTF8=1
export CE_COOK=1
export CE_SURFACE_LIBRARY="$TST_REPO/levels/test/tst/surfaces.json"
export LIGHTMAP_ARGS="--placed-lights"
export CE_START_LIFT=0.1
export TITLE="TST Proving Ground"

bash tools/level/convert_ce_map.sh C:/haloce/hek/maps/tst.map TST C:/haloce/ce_conversions/community/TST
python levels/test/tst/prepare_runtime.py --release-beta
python tools/level/upgrade_ce_map.py TST --work C:/haloce/ce_conversions/community-upgrade
```

Change the TST conversion path in `ce_upgrade_maps.json` when using another
output directory, and pass `prepare_runtime.py --level` accordingly. Run one
editor/cook at a time and do not edit a running build script. The 0.1-CE-unit
spawn lift adds 30.48 cm; check ceiling clearance when changing it.

`CE_SURFACE_LIBRARY` is required for TST's authored architectural finish.
`surfaces.json` supplies the same albedo, roughness, tint and metal values to
Blender and the native cook. `architecture_surfaces.py` assigns real export
slots and writes fitted plate coordinates into UVMap. Omitting the library
uses the stock CE fallback tags and loses the material separation. The cook
owns these shaders under `/Game/MJOLNIR/Maps/TST/SurfaceMaterials`; it does not
require a private replacement for the shared CE runtime. Classic CE uses the
stock fallback materials; the authored PBR finish is a MJOLNIR build feature.

The facility finishes also declare `normal_map`, `normal_convention` and
`normal_strength` (0–1). Use linear tangent-normal data; the example's OpenGL
+Y images are converted once to Unreal's DirectX convention during import.
Keep those texture paths relative to `surfaces.json`, rebuild the Blender
source after a palette edit, and verify the exported role assignments. The
facility source demonstrates these settings; its new cook and game validation
are still pending.

Conversion produces the collision/scenario, materials and meshes. Upgrade
adds the Landscape, scenery, swapped-object collision, foliage, water and world.
Keep all outputs from the same source build together. Watch for missing texture
or shader errors; a successful process exit alone is insufficient.

## 8. Install locally and playtest

Close the game, then use the same tool environment:

```bash
python tools/level/upgrade_ce_map.py TST --stages install --local-install \
  --work C:/haloce/ce_conversions/community-upgrade
```

`--local-install` is for a map the hub does not have yet; with the hub's copy
installed, use `--install`, which puts the build on top of it as local builds.
Both install the checkout's trial masters and loader scripts too. Install the
CE runtime from the launcher first. Back up any prior local map before replacing it.

Oddball and KOTH need mods 0.44.0 or later. Those tests are separate from the
supported-mode beta.

Launch through Steam, reach the main menu and host privately:

```text
mjolnir_auto host TST slayer private
```

Return to the menu before testing `team_slayer` and `ctf`. Test `oddball` and
`koth` only in a development build with their matching code mods. Use
[game automation](game_automation.md) for repeatable captures. Record the game
build, source revision, runtime/code-mod versions and hardware with your results.

| Test | Required evidence |
|---|---|
| Starts | Repeated spawn/death/respawn on both teams without trapping. |
| Slayer | Two players can damage each other, kills score and a round ends. |
| CTF | Both directions: pickup, drop, return, capture and scoring. |
| Oddball | Pickup, timed score, drop/death, abandoned-ball reset and round end. |
| Moving hill | Solo scoring, contested/empty pauses, rotation and round end. |
| Routes | Walk all three routes and each base exit; drive the vehicle route. |
| Collision | Players and bullets stop at expected structure, rock and trunk surfaces. |
| Visuals | Player-height exterior/interior captures; stable water, readable lighting, no seams. |
| Performance | Representative route and fight, with frame times; initial target 60 FPS. |
| Networking | Second machine joins and sees consistent objectives, scores and scenery. |

## 9. Package the first release

`pack_remastered.py` updates existing hub installations. For a new original map,
use `pack_local_map.py`, which reads conversion/upgrade outputs without a hub cache:

```powershell
python tools/level/pack_local_map.py TST `
  --work C:/haloce/ce_conversions/community-upgrade `
  --version 0.1.0-beta.1 --runtime '^1.13.0' `
  --slug tst-proving-ground --name 'TST Proving Ground' `
  --summary 'An editable community custom-map example.' `
  --readme levels/test/tst/BETA.md --size medium --players 2-8 --vehicles true `
  --out C:/haloce/ce_conversions/packages/tst-proving-ground-0.1.0-beta.1.mjolnir `
  --sign
```

The version/range are examples: use versions actually tested. `--cli` selects
your executable. A fresh staging folder is retained beside the archive, and
existing archives are not overwritten. Inspect the world, landscape, meshes,
textures, registration, level file, foliage, decals and referenced water state.

TST's `map_mesh_chunk: true` puts generated cliff, river, capture-bed and shadow
meshes under `/Game/MJOLNIR/Maps/TST/Generated`. A conversion cook and the later
landscape cook can both contain the same paths: if the first contains older
geometry, the game can load it over the new mesh. The upgrade therefore saves
the post-editor map cook, compares generated meshes across the cooked chunks,
and binds the snapshot to the conversion and landscape inputs. Packaging uses
that verified snapshot. Keep inputs unchanged during the build, and inspect the
result in game: a receipt cannot prove arbitrary files came from a given cook.

Before packaging water, host the map, wait for `flux: river filled`, then run
`mjolnir_flux_bake`. Close the game and rerun `--stages assemble`
with the same work directory. This copies the settled state into the build.
Reinstall and verify that the river starts full. Rebake after changing the bed;
matching domain dimensions alone do not prove an old water state is still valid.

The beta advertises only Slayer, Team Slayer and CTF. Additional objective modes
need published, tested rules, loader and HUD support before advertising them.

The hub requires an author signature. Register a device key through the supported
publishing/signing workflow, then add `--sign` to the final packaging command.
Keep private keys out of source and do not alter an archive after signing.
See [map distribution](map_distribution.md) and [archive format](mjolnir_format.md).

## 10. Upload to the hub and verify player installation

Use an authenticated publishing client/API with `mods:write`. This revision's
route prefix is `/api/v1`; do not assume every tag-editor build has a map-upload
button. Check the deployed API's current limits and response schemas.

1. Create a draft with `POST /mods`, supplying `slug`, `name`, `summary`,
   `description_md`, and `category`. Link the exact source revision and guide.
   Reuse an existing listing's slug for an update.
2. Create a release with `POST /mods/{slug}/releases`, supplying a new `version`,
   `channel` (`beta` for playtests), and `changelog_md`. Save the returned ID.
3. Upload the signed archive as raw bytes to `PUT /releases/{id}/archive`.
   This source revision accepts up to 90 MiB in one request. Larger files use
   the multipart routes in `hub/src/lib/api/publish.ts`, with a 1 GiB total cap.
4. Call `POST /releases/{id}/complete`. Read scan findings and status. A successful
   upload is not proof that the release was published.
5. Fix rejected packages, rebuild and re-sign. Some releases require moderator
   review; do not announce them as public while pending.
6. Install from the published listing on a clean player setup. Confirm dependency
   installation, registration, menu visibility, hosting and another player's join.

Release the editable source separately: Blender, JMS, scenario, placements,
scripts, configuration, tool versions, provenance, license/notices and exact
revision. Players need the runtime package; authors need the source and tools.
Publish a new version for fixes so players can identify the build they have.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | First check |
|---|---|
| Hand edits disappeared | Regeneration overwrote generated files; use a separate hand-edited scene and `-SkipGeometry`. |
| HEK lightmap failure | Error geometry, thin Boolean slivers and UV degeneracy; do not reuse the old cache. |
| Scene looks right but collision is wrong | Confirm the collision/BSP and visuals came from the same source build. |
| Only the author can load the map | Inspect package-owned meshes, dependencies and a clean launcher installation. |
| Foliage is washed out under atmospheric sky | Physical sky captures already include sun radiance; do not amplify the capture twice. |
| Objectives appear but do not score | Matching labels, required variant files, code-mod version and active game type. |
| Upload completed but map is not public | Read scan/review status and resolve the reported findings. |


### Native rock material variants

TST's `native_rock_materials` build option preserves the shipped native material
instance, including its compiled layer data, then applies the map's roughness and
coastal color parameters. Build the helper with
`cargo build -p blam-pack --example native_material_clone` before the upgrade bake.
The bake emits `pakchunk970-MJOLNIRROCK-TST_P`; the local installer and packer
require it when that option is enabled. Plain editor-created children of the
placeholder native materials lost the real layer data and rendered black or
white in game; a successful editor cook alone did not catch that failure.
Native game assets remain an installed build dependency, not editable source
files redistributed in this repository.

The TST beta also bakes an ambient cubemap into its world (`MJ_AMBIENT_CUBEMAP` in
`build_ce_landscape.py`). This supplies stable indirect fill with the published loader,
whose realtime sky capture is disabled in the game. The beta disables the runtime
skylight contribution to avoid double lighting; the original CE sky remains visible.

For the enclosed TST pond, the single Adjust source covers the whole water domain
(scale 6, a 60 m footprint). A small source in the middle leaves a visible circular
boundary; removing the source lets the simulated pond drain. Keep its target elevation
at -18 cm so the bank shape controls the shoreline.

guides.title: Your first Forge build
guides.summary: Build a raised courtyard, walk through it as a Spartan, then add the details that make it a playable space: cover, spawns, doors and a route back up. MJOLNIR exposes the game's native Forge editor and adds modular construction packs, a palette and keyboard controls.
guides.body:
Build a raised courtyard, walk through it as a Spartan, then add the details
that make it a playable space: cover, spawns, doors and a route back up.
MJOLNIR exposes the game's native Forge editor and adds modular construction
packs, a palette and keyboard controls.

This guide uses **Foundry Wide 0.2** and MJOLNIRForge's placement controls.
Forge editing is host-only. Use the matching maps and runtime together;
everything in this guide works with mods 0.45.0 or newer (MJOLNIRForge 0.4.2,
MJOLNIRLobby 0.21.0), which the launcher installs and keeps current.

![Foundry Wide's modular construction and utility pieces, rendered in Blender](/docs-images/forge-showcase/foundry-wide.webp)

*Blender render of Foundry Wide. The pack contains 38 pieces; their original
heights remain player-sized while the larger floor and wall modules give you
room to build.*

[Open the full-size Foundry Wide catalog](images/forge-showcase/foundry-wide.webp).

## Choose a place to build

After launching the game, press **Enter** at the title screen and finish
sign-in. From **Multiplayer → Host Game**, choose a map and **Forge**.

For the example below, use **Crossline**: its palette includes
all original Foundry and Foundry Wide pieces. Find a clear area for the build
and leave its existing spawn points intact. **Forge Canvas** is the simpler
64 × 64 m blank starting deck, but its current palette contains original
Foundry, not Foundry Wide. **Roadworks Circuit** is the place to try the
vehicle kit.

A map must include a pack's pieces in its baked palette. Installing another
pack does not automatically add its pieces to every map.

Press **B** to become the Monitor. Use your normal movement and mouse controls
to look around. The target card beside the cursor names the object you are
aiming at or holding; the palette appears on the right.

## Learn the small set of building controls

| Action | Key |
| --- | --- |
| Switch Monitor / Spartan | **B** |
| Choose palette category / item | **Left / Right**, then **Up / Down** |
| Place the selected piece | **Insert** |
| Grab / drop the targeted piece | **V** |
| Bring a held piece closer / move it farther | **Page Down / Page Up** |
| Turn left / right around the vertical axis | **Comma / Period** |
| Duplicate / delete the target | **N / Delete** |
| Change target physics | **F3** |
| Change position grid / rotation increment | **F4 / F10** |
| Save / reload this map's saved layout | **F5 / F6** |
| Restore the map's authored layout | **F2** twice |

Start with **F4: 0.5 m** and **F10: 90°**. These suit the rectangular kit.
The position grid aligns an object's origin when it is placed or dropped;
it does not pull adjacent edges together while you hold it. Rotation controls
turn around the vertical axis only.

For construction, use **F3** to choose **Phased** before dropping a piece.
It stays in position and lets you overlap adjoining geometry. **Fixed** also
stays in position, but contact while carrying it can resist the turn you
requested. **Normal** uses the object's authored physics: a stock weapon can
fall, while a structural model authored with fixed bodies can remain still.
Phased construction still provides the intended player collision.

Check the final orientation after each drop. Native holding motion can settle
slightly away from the requested angle; the grid is a placement aid, not an
automatic model-connection tool. The HUD keeps your current settings visible.

## Build a raised courtyard

This ten-piece exercise creates a **16 × 16 m** courtyard whose walking surface
is **2 m** above the ground. The approach ramp adds another **8 m** of length.
The diagram uses north for the ramp's uphill direction.

![Top-down courtyard recipe: a square raised deck, six walls, two front cover pieces and a broad approach ramp](/docs-images/forge-showcase/courtyard-plan.svg)

| Piece in the Wide palette | Quantity | Size and role |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Wide Floor 4 x 4 | 1 | 16 × 16 × 0.5 m deck |
| Wide Ramp 8 m / Rise 2 m | 1 | 8 × 8 m approach, rising 2 m |
| Wide Wall Full | 6 | 8 × 1 × 3 m walls around three sides |
| Wide Low Cover | 2 | 4 × 1.5 × 1 m front flanks, leaving an 8 m entrance |

1. **Place the floor.** Set it to Phased. Its origin is the centre of its
   underside, so an underside **1.5 m** above the ground puts the walking
   surface at **2 m**. The 0.5 m grid matches both heights.
2. **Connect the ramp.** Set its low end on the ground and turn its high end
   toward the courtyard. Its high edge meets the floor's near edge at 2 m.
   Keep both edges flush; raising the floor's underside to 2 m would create
   a 0.5 m step at the join.
3. **Enclose three sides.** Place two full walls along the back, then two
   along each side. Their bottoms sit on the finished floor. Turn the side
   walls by 90°. Keep their outside faces on the deck's outside edges.
4. **Frame the entrance.** Place one low cover piece on either side of the
   ramp mouth. They leave an 8 m-wide opening and give the courtyard a
   readable front without obstructing the approach.
5. **Walk the route.** Press B, approach from the ground and walk up the
   ramp. Cross the join in both directions, follow the wall edges and check
   that the entrance remains wide enough when you turn into it.
6. **Save a working version.** Press F5 before adding decorative pieces or
   experimenting with a different layout.

For a more exact plan, treat the floor centre as `(0, 0)` and ground as `Z=0`.
These are relative planning coordinates in metres; the editor has no numeric
position-entry panel.

| Piece origins | Position | Turn |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Floor | `(0, 0, 1.5)` | None |
| Ramp | `(0, -12, 0)` | Uphill toward +Y |
| Back walls | `(-4, 7.5, 2)` and `(4, 7.5, 2)` | None |
| Left walls | `(-7.5, -4, 2)` and `(-7.5, 4, 2)` | 90° |
| Right walls | `(7.5, -4, 2)` and `(7.5, 4, 2)` | 90° |
| Front cover | `(-6, -7, 2)` and `(6, -7, 2)` | None |

The [piece reference](../forge-packs/foundry-wide/README.md) has dimensions
for the smaller floors, stairs, corners and bridges. Use them to extend the
same courtyard rather than guessing a piece's size from its thumbnail.

## Give players a way in, out and back into the game

Place **spawn point markers** from the scenery palette on clear walking
surfaces. **K** cycles the target's team between neutral, red and blue.
Keep red and blue starts inside their own bases, with room for a standing
Spartan and a clear first step.

If the map will support **free-for-all Slayer**, include **neutral spawn
markers**. Red and blue starts alone do not cover that mode. Place several
neutral starts around shared areas, away from vehicle traffic and the lift
column. Team games prefer matching initial starts, but can also use neutral
starts for ordinary respawns.

Markers are invisible gameplay objects. Aim close to their position to select
them; V carries a marker and its properties, and N copies it. Leave working
starts in place until you have tested replacements by hosting the intended
game type.

## Add a teleporter route

![The animated green teleporter housing in the game](/docs-images/forge-showcase/portal.webp)

The green housing and pad make the route visible. **Separate native markers
perform the teleport.**

Place a **Teleporter Sender** at the entrance and a **Teleporter Receiver**
at the destination, or use two **Teleporter 2-Way** markers. Target each and
press **P** until both show the same channel. Use another channel for another
route. Turn the destination marker so arrivals face into the playable space.

The Wide pad is 0.5 m thick. Put its underside 0.5 m below the adjoining
finished floor if you want a flush approach, then place the gameplay marker
at the usable entrance. Keep the receiver and the space beyond it clear.
Test both directions as a Spartan. Walk away from the arrival trigger before
trying to return; native teleporters have a rearm distance.

## Make a doorway open automatically

![A vehicle door visibly raised above its frame](/docs-images/forge-showcase/door.webp)

The **frame and panel are separate pieces**. Pair Wide Tall Doorway with
Wide Door Panel, or Wide Vehicle Doorway with Wide Vehicle Door Panel.
Place the frame on a continuous floor, then place the panel at its closed
height. Align their horizontal centres and set the panel 0.75 m toward the
frame's local front (−Y), so it sits just ahead of the frame.

Use **F3: Fixed or Phased** on the panel. Normal disables automatic movement.
Leave clear space for the panel to rise: **4 m** for the infantry door and
**6 m** for the vehicle gate. Static construction above it is not an automatic
stop, so keep the whole travel path clear.

Return to your Spartan and approach. The panel opens, then waits two seconds
after you leave before closing. A nearby player or movable vehicle can keep
it open. Before editing the panel, clear the opening and enter Monitor mode;
if the closing path is occupied, the panel stays raised and its edit waits.
Other pieces remain editable. F5 saves the door's closed design position,
even when the panel is currently open.

## Connect a lift to a gallery

![The lift station's walk-up ramps beside Crossline's raised gallery](/docs-images/forge-showcase/lift.webp)

Place **Wide Lift Station** on the ground with its central column open above.
Its four shallow ramps lead to a deck 0.5 m high. A nearby gallery at **4.5 m**
above the same ground gives this preset a useful landing four metres above
the lift deck.

Keep the landing beside the column rather than directly over it. Walk onto
the centre as a Spartan and steer sideways onto the gallery during the rise.
Staying centred can produce repeated rises. Crossline demonstrates a ground
approach, ascent and controlled gallery landing; use its spacing as a starting
point and test your own geometry. Keep a conventional ramp route available
while you tune the landing.

## Finish with glass, lights and the right scale

![A transparent cyan glass wall in the game](/docs-images/forge-showcase/glass.webp)

Glass walls and glazed windows are transparent, solid and non-breakable.
Use them where players should see a route without walking through it.
Original Foundry's warm, red and blue pylons help distinguish entrances and
team bases. Their lights follow the placed fixtures and currently cast no
shadows.

For vehicles, use the dedicated Roadworks kit. Its **16 m clear roadway**,
24/48 m straights and 40 m-radius curves give a Warthog much more space than
a 4 m-wide pedestrian bridge. The stock vehicle's visual envelope is roughly
6.13 × 3.25 m; leave room to turn, pass and recover as well as fit through.
Road connector positions are documented for authors, but Forge does not
automatically dock them or provide checkpoints and lap timing.

![The Roadworks road kit shown at a consistent presentation scale in Blender](/docs-images/forge-showcase/roadworks.webp)

*Blender render.* [Open the full-size Roadworks catalog](images/forge-showcase/roadworks.webp).

## Save, reload and play

**F5** saves one layout for the current map. **F6** replaces the current
objects with that saved layout, so use it to check that your build restores
correctly. **F2**, pressed twice, returns to the map's authored layout and
preserves the old save in history; **F6** then brings that save back.

A saved layout also applies when you host that map as Slayer or another game
type. Return through the lobby and try the mode you intend people to play:
check its spawns, walk every join, use both teleporter directions and try the
doors as a Spartan. Door layouts should be saved by the host; a session that
changes host needs a rehost before door automation and saves resume.

Keep a layout's `.mvar` and `.mvar.packs` files together when backing it up.
The companion records the pack identities the layout needs. Matching pack
versions matter: changing a model or palette can change what an old placement
means. The launcher dependency workflow handles declared pack requirements;
copying a lone layout file is not a substitute for those assets.

For the full key and property reference, see [Forge controls](forge.md).
To create your own models and submit a pack, continue with the
[community pack authoring guide](forge_pack_authoring.md). The
[utility reference](forge_pack_utilities.md) describes door, lift and surface
metadata; the [validation record](forge_pack_validation.md) keeps the detailed
test evidence separate from this building guide.

guides.title: Create a community Forge pack
guides.summary: A Forge pack adds your models to the pieces a map can offer in Forge. You can contribute model sources and work with a maintainer on integration, or build a complete .mjolnir content archive yourself. A small, well-tested set of floors, walls and ramps is a useful first…
guides.body:
A Forge pack adds your models to the pieces a map can offer in Forge. You can
contribute **model sources** and work with a maintainer on integration, or build
a complete **`.mjolnir` content archive** yourself. A small, well-tested set of
floors, walls and ramps is a useful first contribution.

The Hub's Forge catalog lists packs, and the launcher resolves the published
releases a map or saved layout requires. This guide takes your source models
through the build, test, signing and submission workflow. If you want to focus
on modelling, a source pull request lets you work with a maintainer on the
remaining steps.

For building a level with existing pieces, start with the
[Forge building guide](forge_guide.md). This page is for making the pieces.

## Design a set that fits together

Choose a module and keep mating faces exact. Foundry uses a 2 m module;
[Foundry Wide](../forge-packs/foundry-wide/README.md) uses 4 m. A useful Wide-scale
starter set might contain an 8 × 8 m floor, an 8 m wall, a doorway and an
8 m-wide ramp. Make the ramp end at an existing floor height. A 0.5 m floor
edge can block walking even when the player fits on top; use a flush transition
or a shallow access ramp.

Author in **metres, right-handed Z up**. Bottom-centre origins work well for
buildings: the bottom face is Z = 0, and adjoining pieces share predictable
coordinates. Roads may use an entry connector as their origin; document that
choice and keep it consistent. Use a separate presentation layout for renders
so a contact sheet's scale never becomes the exported asset's scale.

Check clear space against actual game scale. The standing Spartan collision
shape is about **1.98 m high and 1.07 m across**. The assembled Warthog visual
envelope is about **6.13 × 3.25 × 2.43 m**; roads also need turning room and
space beside the vehicle. The [scale reference](../forge-packs/roadworks/SCALE.md)
records the measurements. An opening that barely fits a static box is not a
verified drivable route.

Keep the visible mesh and collision separate. A doorway needs separate jamb
and header hulls, not one solid box around its outside. Use closed, outward-wound
convex collision hulls and retain real holes between them. Small bevels and trim
can remain visual details while collision faces meet exactly. The current
collision cooker accepts at most 4,096 triangles per piece; the physics builder
accepts at most 256 convex hulls, with additional plane/vector bounds. Start
well below those limits and test the shapes you actually ship.

The catalog's `snap_m` is a suggestion, not automatic connector docking or a
per-piece editor setting. Forge's position grid and rotation controls are
described in the [building guide](forge_guide.md).

## Contribute models without building the runtime pack

Open a source pull request with a small folder under `forge-packs/<your-slug>/`.
Include the editable model source or reproducible generator, a preview, intended
dimensions and origin, and a short explanation of how the pieces join. Keep
authoring sources outside ignored `build/` directories. If native collision or
the exporter is unfinished, say so in the PR; a model contribution can be reviewed
without pretending it is already an installable pack.

State who made the geometry, which assets you reused, and their licenses. The
reference geometry and implementation use the repository's MIT license. A game
texture's presence in an installed game does not make it part of that license.
Separate original art from game-derived build inputs, and keep extracted game
files out of the source contribution. Preview images should say whether they
are Blender renders or actual gameplay captures.

Use [Foundry's generator and exporter](../forge-packs/foundry/README.md) as a
working reference, and [Foundry Wide](../forge-packs/foundry-wide/README.md) for
larger pieces. The existing Blender scripts regenerate their source meshes;
editing their generated `.blend` alone will not change the next build. A custom
Blender workflow needs an exporter that produces the inputs below. There is no
general-purpose `.blend` drag-and-drop importer into the game.

## Give the pack stable identities

Choose your own namespace rather than changing a reference pack's ID. For
example, a one-piece `courtyard-kit` catalog could begin as follows:

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "name": "Courtyard Kit",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "type": "content",
  "summary": "Modular courtyard floors and boundaries",
  "forge_pack": {
    "schema_version": 1,
    "id": "courtyard-kit",
    "blocks": [
      {
        "id": "floor_8x8",
        "name": "Courtyard Floor 8 x 8",
        "tag": "objects\\mjolnir\\forge\\courtyard-kit\\floor_8x8",
        "category": "floors",
        "dimensions_m": [8, 8, 0.5],
        "snap_m": 0.5
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

This is metadata, not a complete model. Save the authoring catalog as
`catalog.json`; the builder writes the release manifest as `mjolnir.json`.
The pack ID must match its eventual Hub slug: 2–64 lowercase letters, digits
or hyphens, starting with a letter or digit. Block IDs and categories also
allow underscores and may be 1–64 characters. Block names are nonblank and at
most 80 characters. Dimensions and optional snap are finite positive metres.

Every block tag must be exactly `objects\mjolnir\forge\<pack-id>\<block-id>`.
Keep IDs stable, and add new entries after existing ones when maintaining a
map's palette. Every change gets a new semantic version; versions cannot
contain `+build` metadata, and published bytes never change under the same
version.

Plan updates as SemVer lines ([updating a pack](forge_packs.md#updating-a-pack)).
Maps and saved layouts built with a release keep working with any later
release in its line, so within a line keep every existing piece's ID, kind,
dimensions, snap, origin and join heights. Fix a piece's look or collision
within that shape, or add pieces, in the next release of the line: a patch
release before 1.0 (`0.2.0` to `0.2.1`), a minor or patch one after it. To
change or remove a piece, start a new line (`0.3.0`, or `2.0.0`), and expect
maps and layouts that use it to be rebuilt. The Hub refuses a release that
drops or resizes a piece of an earlier release in its line.

Catalog entries are building blocks for now. `kind` names are reserved for
scenery, weapons, vehicles, equipment and bipeds, and a `requires` list for
features later launchers add; packs using either are refused until MJOLNIR
supports them ([entry kinds](forge_packs.md#entry-kinds)).

Ordinary pieces need no behavior metadata. Optional lights, lifts, doors and
approved glass/portal surfaces are described in the
[utility contract](forge_pack_utilities.md). These fields select bounded runtime
features; they do not let a pack install arbitrary Lua, DLLs or actor paths.
A decorative teleporter housing still needs native gameplay markers and a
channel. New executable behavior belongs in a separate
[reviewed code contribution](contributing_code_mods.md).

## Build a complete local pack

First reproduce the [Foundry build recipe](forge_packs.md#build-the-foundry-content)
with the supported game/runtime files. It builds the CLI and its helper tools,
exports Blender models, and cooks the native collision and physics.
The current builder is a developer tool, not a one-click modeling application.

For a custom pack, provide these matching inputs:

| Input | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `catalog.json` | Release identity and block catalog |
| `source/geometry.json` | `units: "meters"`, `axes: "right_handed_z_up"`, and matching piece IDs with visual meshes and collision |
| `build/models/<id>.gltf` and its buffers | Exported metre-scale visual mesh; the reference Blender exporter writes standard Y-up glTF |
| `build/blam-collision/<id>.collision_model` | Cooked native triangle collision |
| `build/blam-collision/<id>.physics_model` | Cooked native convex physics |

The source geometry contains a `pieces` list. Each piece supplies visual
components and an aggregate collision mesh plus its individual convex hulls.
Follow the reference generators' format rather than renaming an arbitrary glTF
and assuming collision will be inferred. The ordinary builder maps its known
material names (`concrete`, `deck`, `gunmetal`, `amber`, and light lenses) to
shipped materials. Custom Blender shaders do not automatically become game
materials. Approved glass and portal profiles require the separate
[material cook](forge_pack_materials.md), including a nonconflicting shader chunk.

Once your source geometry and visual exports exist, these are the actual
custom-pack cooking commands. Run from the repository root and substitute your
pack and local input paths. `$paks` must contain the supported game and runtime
donors; keep it separate from build output. The builder uses hardlinks, so its
input view and output need to be on the same filesystem volume.

```powershell
$slug = 'courtyard-kit'
$pack = "forge-packs/$slug"
$paks = 'C:/local/base-and-runtime-paks'
$cli = 'target/debug/mjolnir.exe'

& $cli extract --paks $paks --group collision_model --filter crate_space_a `
  --shipped-only --verify --out "$pack/build/donors"
$donor = "$pack/build/donors/objects/props/covenant/crate_space_a/crate_space_a.collision_model"
cargo run -p blam-sbsp --example forge_collision -- `
  "$pack/source/geometry.json" $donor "$pack/build/blam-collision"
python tools/forge/build_collision.py "$pack/source/geometry.json" `
  "$pack/build/blam-physics" --mjolnir $cli --paks $paks --pack-id $slug `
  --payload-out "$pack/build/blam-collision"
python tools/forge/build_pack.py $pack --paks $paks

& $cli forge pack "$pack/build/game/all/mjolnir.json" `
  --content "$pack/build/game/all/content" --readme "$pack/README.md" `
  --changes "$pack/build/game/all/changes.json" `
  --out "$pack/build/courtyard-kit-0.1.0.mjolnir"
```

The final command creates an **unsigned local test archive**. It does not
install files or upload anything. `build_pack.py --only <block-id>` builds a
small diagnostic set under `build/game/<block-id>/`; do not publish that subset
as though it were the complete pack. Builders retain outputs, so use a fresh
build workspace when changing input versions or removing pieces.

## Make a test map and test the result

A map must explicitly declare the pack version and block IDs in
`blam.forge_packs`, then be baked as a standalone map with those cooked pack
containers in its input view. Follow [adding a pack to a map](forge_packs.md#add-a-pack-to-a-map)
and [level authoring](level_authoring.md). Installing a pack alone does not add
its pieces to an existing map, and there is no automatic map rebake.

A pack can describe 1–256 pieces, but a map can select at most 200 custom
references from at most 63 packs, within the engine's 255 total palette entries.
The selected subset and order belong to the map. The launcher accepts at most
4,096 enabled catalog blocks across a profile. Those are different limits;
making a larger catalog does not increase a map's palette capacity.

In a private test map, check rendering, scale, visible and physical openings,
ramp joins, and ordinary walking onto raised pieces. Try placing, grabbing,
rotating, duplicating, deleting and reloading each type. Test the intended game
modes too: free-for-all needs neutral spawn scenery, not only red/blue markers
or campaign starting locations. Record what passed and what remains untested.
The [reference validation record](forge_pack_validation.md) separates offline
checks, Blender previews and live-game evidence.

Map archives depend on the line of each pack they were baked with (`^0.2.0`).
Saved layouts use both `.mvar` and `.mvar.packs`; keep the pair together. The
launcher resolves missing published releases before launch and refuses a pack
outside the line a map or layout needs. A changed installed
pack requires a restart. Include a clean launcher profile in release testing
so you also check downloads and dependency resolution.

## Sign and submit a release

For a release, rerun `mjolnir forge pack` with **`--sign`**. This uses the device
key created by the tag editor, run as the same Windows user. Its public key
must be registered to the Hub account that uploads the release. Registration
is part of the editor's configured publishing flow; creating a local key alone
does not register it. Advanced builds may use `--sign-seed <file>` instead, with
that public key registered first. Keep private seeds and credentials out of
the contribution. See [archive signing](mod_signing_design.md).

Create a content listing on the Hub's **New mod** page (`/mods/new`), with the
Forge pack category and the same slug as `forge_pack.id`. Create the matching version on
its manage page and upload the signed `.mjolnir` archive. The scanner verifies
the signature, identity, archive contents, catalog and required surface packages;
scan failures must be fixed before publication. Selecting a category alone does
not create a valid Forge pack.

Source PRs receive maintainer review. Hub releases follow the site's scan and
moderation rules; the current automatic prepublication review queue applies to
maps from new/untrusted authors, not every content pack. Publish a small tested release with
clear provenance and limitations, then expand it while preserving the identities
that other people's maps and layouts depend on.

guides.title: Driving the Game From Outside
guides.summary: Every experiment in this repository used to end at the same place: build the thing, then sit in front of the game and type at it. Load a level, alt-tab, run a command, read a number off the screen, write it down. That is slow, it is easy to get wrong, and it means no experiment…
guides.body:
**Status:** Working on CU4 (`2026.08.11.1121610.2-Rel-i343-Meteorite-2607-CU4`, Steam), which the tools have driven since 2026-08-18. First verified end to end on 2026-07-27 on CU2; the Hazards below say what changed. See [`build_lock.md`](build_lock.md).

Every experiment in this repository used to end at the same place: build the thing, then sit in
front of the game and type at it. Load a level, alt-tab, run a command, read a number off the
screen, write it down. That is slow, it is easy to get wrong, and it means no experiment can be
repeated cheaply enough to be worth repeating.

This is the fix. The game becomes something a tool can drive: launch it, start a mission, run
console commands, evaluate Lua inside the process, send keys and mouse, and take screenshots.

## The shape of it

Three transports, because no single one reaches everything.

| | Reaches | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **Bridge mod** | Lua and console commands inside the process | [`mods/MJOLNIRBridge`](../mods/MJOLNIRBridge/Scripts/main.lua) |
| **capture.ps1** | What is on screen | [`tools/mcp/game/capture.ps1`](../tools/mcp/game/capture.ps1) |
| **input.ps1** | Menus, anything needing real input (player movement unverified on CU4, see Hazards) | [`tools/mcp/game/input.ps1`](../tools/mcp/game/input.ps1) |

[`tools/mcp/game/game.mjs`](../tools/mcp/game/game.mjs) is the tools themselves.
[`server.mjs`](../tools/mcp/game/server.mjs) serves them over MCP and
[`cli.mjs`](../tools/mcp/game/cli.mjs) runs them from a shell. Both are thin, so anything one
can do the other can too — which matters when something breaks and you need to run a single
step by hand.

**Prefer the bridge over screenshots.** A value read by reflection is exact. A value read off
pixels is a guess about pixels, and the guess is usually right, which is what makes it
dangerous.

## Setup

```bash
node tools/mcp/game/cli.mjs status
```

If it says the bridge mod is not installed, install MJOLNIRBridge from the launcher's **My Mods**
page (*Available to install*), or from a clone:

```powershell
.\scripts\install-bridge.ps1
```

That copies the mod into the game's UE4SS `Mods` folder, enables it in `mods.txt` above the
`Keybinds` entry that has to stay last, and creates the directory the bridge talks through.
Nothing shipped is modified; deleting the mod folder and its `mods.txt` line undoes all of it.
Re-run it after editing the Lua — UE4SS reads mods from disk at startup, so copy and restart is
the whole edit loop.

The tools find a Steam install from Steam's own library index. Set `MJOLNIR_GAME_DIR` for any
other; for the Xbox app (Game Pass) it is the install's `Content` folder, whose binaries are
`WinGDK`. `install-bridge.ps1` handles Steam (`Win64`) installs only.

`.mcp.json` registers the MCP server. Claude Code loads it at session start, so a session
already running will not see it until it restarts.

## The tools

| Tool | Does |
|---|---|
| `game_status` | Install, process, bridge heartbeat, current world and pawn |
| `game_launch` | Start it and wait until the bridge answers |
| `game_quit` | Close it |
| `game_display` | Window mode, or restore the user's own settings |
| `game_console` | A UE console command through the local `PlayerController` |
| `game_lua` | Evaluate Lua on the game thread, return what it printed |
| `game_travel` | `open` a level — see the hazard below |
| `game_screenshot` | Photograph the window |
| `game_input` | Drive the player from inside the game: key, hold, mouse button, `move` look, `release`, `wait` steps. `method: "sendinput"` goes through the desktop instead, for menus, and adds absolute `click` |
| `game_log` | Tail `UE4SS.log` |

`game_lua` is the one that matters. Tag values, ammo, pawn state and loaded assets are all
reachable by reflection but not through any fixed command, so the useful shape is an eval rather
than a menu of verbs. Helpers are pre-bound: `mj.pc()`, `mj.pawn()`, `mj.world()`,
`mj.find(class)`, `mj.props(obj)`, `mj.name(obj)`, `mj.console(cmd)`. UE4SS reflection —
`FindAllOf`, `StaticFindObject`, `FName` — is there too. The sandbox persists between calls, so
a helper defined once stays defined.

Long scripts come from stdin:

```bash
node tools/mcp/game/cli.mjs lua --timeout=60000 < scan.lua
```

## The wire

UE4SS's Lua has no sockets, so the bridge uses files both sides can open, in
`<install>/Meteorite/Binaries/Win64/ue4ss/mjolnir-bridge/`. Length-prefixed bodies, LF only, so
a body can contain anything including the header delimiter:

```
mjolnir-bridge 1
id 42
op lua
bytes 17
--
print("hello")
```

`request.txt` in, `response.txt` out, and `status.txt` as a heartbeat written about once a
second. The heartbeat is what makes failures legible: `now` is stamped by the poll thread and
`refreshed` by the game thread, so the gap between them says whether the game is hung, loading,
or fine. A caller that times out can tell the difference between "the mod is not loaded" and
"the game thread is busy", which are very different problems.

## What is verified

Run on 2026-07-27, in this order, all of it without touching the keyboard:

1. `game_launch` → Steam → title screen, bridge answering in about 90 seconds.
2. `game_screenshot` → the title screen, captured by `PrintWindow` **without stealing focus**.
3. `game_input` (`sendinput`) Enter, Enter → through login and into mission A30 from the resume slot.
4. `game_lua` → 37,409 loaded objects enumerated, pawn and world named.
5. `game_console` → `stat fps`, dispatched via the Kismet fallback, visible in the next capture.
6. `game_input` → fire and reload, and the HUD reflected it.

For automated multiplayer or Forge tests after a fresh launch, clear the
**PRESS ENTER TO START** screen and finish sign-in before issuing
`mjolnir_auto host`. Wait for `MULTIPLAYER is on the main menu` in the current
`UE4SS.log`; `tools/remote/jip-test.mjs` also checks `signed_in` before hosting.
Starting from the title screen can load the Unreal world and its pawn while
the native simulation remains inactive, producing a black scene. This was
reproduced with an unchanged Roadworks installation on 2026-11-02; signing
in first restored normal play. See the [startup investigation](multiplayer_investigation_notes.md).

The capture path is worth calling out, and the 2026-07-27 reading of it was too generous.

**`PrintWindow` captures the UI layer only — the 3D scene comes back black.** Verified
2026-08-03 in a live A30 mission: the default capture returned a correct HUD (objective text,
reticle, radar, ammo) over a completely black frame, while `game_screenshot` with
`foreground: true` — the `CopyFromScreen` path — showed the actual forest, cliffs and weapon
model in the same instant. The D3D12 swapchain is not in what `PrintWindow` composites; Slate is.

This matters more than it sounds, because a black frame with a working HUD reads exactly like a
rendering failure in the game. It cost the custom-world investigation a documented "runtime-
spawned geometry does not render" dead end that was never real. **When a capture is meant to
show the world rather than the interface, pass `foreground: true`** and accept the focus steal.
`CopyFromScreen` needs the window genuinely frontmost; if the frame comes back showing desktop
or another window, send any `game_input` step with `method: "sendinput"` first to raise it, then capture.

Screenshots are for looking at the world. For anything countable, `game_lua` is exact.

Screenshots default to **800 px wide**, from a game launched at 1280x720. Cost scales with area,
so the difference between 800 and 1600 is four times the tokens for the same frame; 800 is still
comfortably enough to read HUD counters. Raise `max_width` for genuinely small text.

### Silent local video capture (experimental)

For a moving-camera study, `tools/mcp/game/record_game.py` records the visible game
client rectangle to a local MP4. It uses FFmpeg's `gdigrab` desktop source because
this game's D3D12 world is not reliably present in window-DC capture. It selects
the game's `UnrealWindow` by class and process, as `capture.ps1` does, and checks
that the window remains in the foreground at the same position and size. It
does not change OBS, stream, capture audio, or draw the pointer. The existing
MJOLNIRFlyCam F8 control hides the HUD and first-person rig for clean footage;
F8 again restores them.

Install the optional FFmpeg executable only in the ignored working directory,
then create a new destination for each take:

```powershell
python -m pip install --target .dream-loop/video-deps imageio-ffmpeg==0.6.0
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force .dream-loop/video-test | Out-Null
python tools/mcp/game/record_game.py .dream-loop/video-test/shot-001.mp4 `
  --duration 10 --fps 60 --encoder h264_nvenc --start-delay 5 `
  --ready-file .dream-loop/video-test/shot-001.ready.json
```

Switch to the game during the five-second delay and leave it visible and in
front until recording ends. Use `--encoder libx264` on a machine without a
working NVIDIA encoder. An explicit `--ffmpeg` path or a PATH installation may
be used instead of `video-deps`. The optional ready file is created only after
the first encoded frame; a camera driver can wait for that file before starting
its path. Use a fresh ready-file name per take and confirm the recorder is still
running: a ready file left by an interrupted take is not proof of success.

Output and ready files must not already exist. The recorder writes a uniquely
named partial MP4 first and publishes the requested name only after FFmpeg exits
successfully and a frame can be decoded. Losing focus, minimizing, moving or
resizing the game stops the recording and leaves the partial file for diagnosis.
The foreground check runs every 50 ms, so it is not a privacy boundary: system
overlays or notifications can appear in the recorded rectangle, and a brief focus
change may be captured before detection. Review a clip before sharing. Check the
actual image and frame cadence; requested FPS is not a guarantee, especially for
4K GDI capture under load. A private TST beta test recorded a HUD-free moving
camera at 1280×720 with NVENC and a 30 FPS request; framing was inspected at
several points. Higher resolutions, sustained frame cadence and other display
configurations still need verification.

## Hazards

**`open` from the frontend menu crashes the game — and solo-to-solo travel does too.**
Verified: `EXCEPTION_ACCESS_VIOLATION` reading `0x1c`, a couple of minutes into the load.
`open` skips the setup the campaign flow performs. `game_travel` refuses from the frontend
unless forced, but the 2026-08-02 resize experiment hit the identical crash travelling
`open a30` from *inside* mission A15, so treat solo-to-solo travel as unsafe too. Start
missions through the menus with `game_input` (`sendinput`): the resume slot is two Enters from launch, and
mission select is Campaign → New Game → difficulty → mission → two Enters through the skulls
screen (Enter is "start" there — Space toggles the hovered skull, so keep the cursor off
Bandana). That was CU2. **On CU4 the frontend menu's items ignore Enter and take only the
mouse** (2026-08-18): use `{"click":[x,y]}` steps, which place the cursor absolutely in
window-client pixels, so scale up from the 800 px screenshot. Relative `move` steps go through
pointer acceleration and miss. The two-PC harness signs in with Enter, a click at the window
centre, then Space (`SIGN_IN` in [`tools/remote/jip-test.mjs`](../tools/remote/jip-test.mjs)).

The multiplayer notes had already flagged `mjolnir_travel` as unverified and recommended
reusing the official campaign flow. This is that prediction coming true.

**Long work on the game thread freezes the game.** Walking every property of all 37,000 loaded
objects ran past three minutes and the game was unresponsive throughout. It recovers, and the
heartbeat keeps ticking because the poll thread is separate, but scans should be narrowed to
candidate classes first.

**A hung game thread fails fast.** The game window belongs to the game thread, so
`game_screenshot` and `game_input` refuse when the heartbeat shows that thread 15 s behind,
rather than block on it. A capture script still running after 20 s is killed, and an input
script 20 s past its own waits and holds. A bridge call returns as soon as the game process is
gone, rather than waiting out its timeout.

**`game_input` drives the player from inside the game by default.** The simulation reads each
frame's keys, mouse look and buttons through one virtual method in the exe, and that method empties
them unless the local player's viewport has focus. `native/test_input` hooks its vtable slot and adds
test input after that check: no OS input, no focus change, and the game can sit in the background.
It is for tests only. Nothing loads the DLL until `game_input` runs, and neither CI nor a release
builds it. Run `native/test_input/build.ps1`, then `scripts/install-bridge.ps1` with the game closed.
If the DLL is missing the tool fails; it never falls back to SendInput by itself. The reply counts
the simulation's reads during the call: zero means no simulation is running, or the hook is not on
the object it reads. This route reaches the player only: menus are Unreal widgets and never see it.
It was built from reading the exe, with an offline test against the exe on disk. It has driven
the player in real matches since the two-PC run of 2026-11-07, and `tools/bot` plays whole matches
through it.

**`method: "sendinput"` steals focus, and needs an unlocked machine.** It is for menus and other
screens that need the real cursor. Posted messages do not work and the window has to be in front.
Windows also refuses `SetForegroundWindow` to a process that does not already own the foreground, so
the tool taps Alt and attaches to the foreground window's input queue to get around it, retrying as
the window settles.

None of that helps if the workstation is **locked, on a screensaver, or a disconnected Remote
Desktop session**: the interactive desktop is switched away, `GetForegroundWindow` returns 0, and
no synthetic input can reach the game. RDP is the one that bites in practice — the session locks
on idle timeout, and since the automation is doing the work nobody is touching the machine to keep
it alive. Expect to hit this on any run longer than the timeout.
`game_input` reports this as a focus warning rather than pretending it worked. Screenshots keep
working throughout, because `PrintWindow` does not need focus — so a locked machine looks like
"I can see the game but cannot touch it".

**Whether SendInput moves the player is disputed.** A CU4 session on 2026-09-11 recorded it as
driving menus only. On 2026-11-04 real presses reached a player in a match
(`docs/re/ce_map_scripts.md`). What feeds the game's keyboard handler is still open, so a player who
does not move under `sendinput` says nothing about the map.

**Do not judge player movement by `mj.pawn()`.** That is the UE pawn, whose location stays constant,
so it cannot show whether the player moved. Read the `BP_SpartansBipedActor_C` actor or the camera
instead.

~~There is no reflection-driven substitute yet.~~ **Superseded 2026-08-02:** there is one.
`BlamCampaignFlowGameSubsystem:SetAndBeginCampaign(Campaign, ScenarioName, Options)` starts a
mission from pure reflection — verified launching A15 from the frontend and traveling A15→A30
mid-mission on CU3. It validates assets synchronously and returns `false` instead of crashing
when a world is missing, which also retires the frontend-`open` hazard for mission starts. The
game's own hidden debug menu (`WBP_MainMenu:OnToggleDebugMenu`) drives the same path. See
[`multiplayer_investigation_notes.md`](multiplayer_investigation_notes.md) for the full recipe;
`mjolnir_mission` in `MJOLNIRMultiplayer` wraps it.

**Update 2026-10-21:** on CU4 (found 2026-08-19), from the frontend, `mjolnir_mission` is
accepted and the world loads, but the Blam session never comes up and the mission never starts
([`multiplayer_investigation_notes.md`](multiplayer_investigation_notes.md)); `mjolnir level
bake` prints the same warning. So the frontend hazard stands for cold starts: start campaign
missions through the game's own menu with `game_input` (`sendinput`) clicks. Multiplayer maps start from
MJOLNIRLobby (see "Matches and a second PC" below).

**Ammo is not in UE reflection.** Neither the pawn, the first-person weapon actor, nor any HUD
object holds the round counts the HUD displays; a scan for the literal reserve value across
every loaded object found nothing. It lives in the Blam simulation, consistent with tag payloads
being opaque blobs parsed natively. Read it from a screenshot, or find the native path.

**`game_launch` edits `GameUserSettings.ini`** to force windowed mode, because that is the only
lever that works whatever route the game starts by — Steam's `rungameid` URL is not a reliable
way to pass `-windowed`. The original is copied to `GameUserSettings.ini.mjolnir-backup` on the
first change; `game_display` with `mode: restore` puts it back.

**The Steam app id is 2806050**, per `apps/launcher` and Steam's own `appmanifest_2806050.acf`.
The README carried 2993530 for a while, which is a different app and gets "game not found" on
launch; it has been corrected.

## Matches and a second PC

MJOLNIRLobby answers `mjolnir_auto <verb>` at the console and writes its answer to
`native\auto_state.txt` in the mod's folder, so a script can host and join without anyone at
the menus: `state`, `host <CODE> <mode> [private]`, `public on|off`, `join [host]`,
`download <CODE>` and `install <CODE>`. `host` lists the game publicly unless given `private`,
and a listed game is joinable by anyone on the hub, so solo tests use `private`.

After every fresh launch, clear **PRESS ENTER TO START** and wait for the stock
main menu before hosting. A responsive bridge or a signed-in hub identity is
not sufficient: skipping the stock login/profile initialization can load the
Unreal map while the Blam mission never starts. `mjolnir_auto state` must report
`signed_in=1`; `host` refuses earlier requests without changing the map or
starting a countdown. The readiness flag survives MJOLNIR menu overlays and
post-game voting, and resets when the title screen becomes active again.
For input-free sign-in, `remote.mjs signin` calls the title screen's own click
event and waits for `MULTIPLAYER is on the main menu`. The two-PC test's
`signIn()` step performs this prerequisite before hosting.

[`tools/remote/remote.mjs`](../tools/remote/remote.mjs) drives a second PC's game through
[`tools/remote/mjolnir-agent.ps1`](../tools/remote/mjolnir-agent.ps1) running there: status,
Lua, console, input, `mjolnir_auto` and files, over the LAN with a token (`MJOLNIR_REMOTE` and
`MJOLNIR_REMOTE_TOKEN`, or `%USERPROFILE%\.mjolnir-remote.json`). It also drives the player from
inside that game (`game-input`), reads its objects (`objects`), moves a player (`teleport`),
signs in (`signin`) and installs or removes hub mods through the launcher
(`launcher install|uninstall`); the script's header lists every command.

Two more tools build on these. [`tools/remote/instances.mjs`](../tools/remote/instances.mjs)
runs two to four copies of the game on one PC, each with its own saves (`game_launch`'s
`save_suffix`; see [`multi_instance.md`](multi_instance.md) in the repository).
[`tools/bot/`](../tools/bot/README.md) plays a match as a player, driving the in-game input
route along the map's navigation mesh.

The agent also brings that PC up to date through its own MJOLNIR launcher (agent 8). Run
`remote.mjs launcher update` with the game closed. It starts the launcher with WebView2's
debugging port (bound to 127.0.0.1), opens Updates and presses **Update all**, using
[`tools/remote/launcher.ps1`](../tools/remote/launcher.ps1). The launcher's own order applies:
it updates itself, restarts, then installs the core, the code mods and the hub mods. Progress is
read from the launcher's `--check-updates`. A launcher older than 0.17.0 can't answer that, so
for one of those the Updates screen is read until it has updated itself. The script never
presses Launch, because a launch puts back the released files of any code mod whose files
were replaced by hand, undoing a test copy. (Folders whose names start with `MJOLNIR` are never
set aside.) Afterwards,
one-off test files go on with `put` and `sync-mods.mjs` as before, and stay until the next
update. `launcher check` lists what is out of date without changing anything; `launcher status`
shows the installed version and the last run.
[`tools/remote/jip-test.mjs`](../tools/remote/jip-test.mjs) runs the two-PC join-in-progress
test end to end with both.
